rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and critical pairs. The high final organic fraction limits the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Change temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity in the crowded central cluster and late doublet. The short initial elution window leaves ample room for subsequent gradient expansion.

Flatten the gradient at the more promising temperature to expand the crowded groups and test slope-dependent selectivity. The previous last peak at 4.71 minutes suggests substantial room to improve separation before the time penalty becomes important.

The shallower gradient resolved the central cluster, leaving only one close pair. Lower temperature by one step to shift that pair’s selectivity while retaining the successful gradient and likely staying below ten minutes.

Increase the starting organic fraction to test selectivity of the remaining close central pair while making the gradient shallower. This should also move the elution window earlier, preserving room for further slope refinement without a time penalty.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining central separation at 55 °C. A modest increase in starting organic fraction should offset much of the added retention time without compressing the early cluster as strongly as the previous run.

At 60 °C the central pair separated better; a substantially shallower gradient will test whether the other critical pair separates after its apparent selectivity crossover. Raising the starting organic fraction should keep the last peak near or below ten minutes.

Scout the low-temperature selectivity regime, since 55–60 °C trades separation of one critical pair against another. A moderately shorter gradient should limit the retention-time increase while revealing whether cooling separates the central cluster more effectively.

Keep the promising low-temperature selectivity and increase starting organic by one step to bring the last peak below ten minutes. The slightly shallower gradient may also lift the near-resolved central pair above R = 1.5.

Shorten the nearly successful low-temperature method by one gradient step to remove its small time penalty. This also tests whether a steeper gradient improves the marginal central pair, whose resolution declined in the previous shallower-gradient run.

Lengthen injection 9’s gradient by one step to raise the marginal central pair above R = 1.5. Its 9.25-minute last peak leaves enough headroom that this modest extension is expected to retain all peaks within ten minutes.

The maximum CRF is secured; now increase starting organic by one step to seek a shorter fully resolved method. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed to test whether the current resolution margin survives the earlier elution window.

Raise temperature by one step to test a shorter elution window while retaining the successful gradient. The central pair has little resolution margin, so this run will establish whether warming is a viable route to further shortening.

Return to 25 °C and raise starting organic to move peaks earlier, compensating with a shallower gradient to protect the central pair. This tests whether a narrower effective gradient window can shorten the fully resolved method beyond injection 12.

At the previous gradient, warming improved the central pair but compressed its preceding neighbor. Injection 14 gives that neighbor more separation, so one temperature step may now resolve both while bringing the last peak earlier.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the sole under-resolved central pair in injection 15. Monitor the neighboring and final pairs, which have limited margin, while seeking full resolution with the last peak still well below ten minutes.

Return to 25 °C to restore the final pair’s separation while retaining the shallower gradient needed by the central pair. This should test a fully resolved alternative near nine minutes, with injection 12 retained as the shortest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test the next temperature step for a selectivity crossover that could restore full separation at a shorter retention time. The maximum score is already secured, so this run explores a faster alternative rather than extending the low-temperature gradient.

Test a warmer selectivity regime beyond the central-cluster crossover seen at 30–35 °C. Holding the gradient fixed isolates temperature effects and may reveal a fully resolved alternative faster than the confirmed 8.90-minute method.

Flatten the promising 45 °C gradient to improve its two marginal pairs. The last peak at 7.03 minutes leaves room for this extension while potentially yielding a faster fully resolved method than injection 12.

Return to the near-resolved 30 °C regime and shorten its gradient by one step. A steeper slope may separate the compressed early pair while retaining enough resolution in its neighbor, potentially achieving full resolution below eight minutes.

Preserve injection 16’s initial gradient slope but transition to a hold after the central cluster elutes. This targets the sole unresolved late pair through altered late-stage selectivity while aiming to keep the last peak below ten minutes.

Return to the reliable 25 °C selectivity and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to protect the central pair. This explores another potentially shorter fully resolved window while retaining injection 12 as the best confirmed fast method.

Refine the shortest confirmed maximum-score method by slightly reducing its gradient slope to build resolution margin above the borderline R = 1.52. The 1.10-minute headroom below the time-penalty threshold should accommodate this modest retention increase.

Use a slope between injections 12 and 24 to shorten the latter’s elution window while preserving more resolution margin than injection 12. This final refinement targets the maximum CRF with all peaks below ten minutes and the critical pair comfortably above R = 1.5.
